title: Suasoriae
author: Seneca the Elder
source: Translated by Claude from phi1014.phi003.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Corruptissimam rem omnium quae umquam dictae sunt ex quo homines diserti insanire coeperunt, putabant Dorionis esse in metaphrasi dictam Homeri, cum excaecatus Cyclops saxum in mare reiecit Haec quomodo ex corruptis eo perueniant, ut et magna et tamen sana sint, aiebat Maecenas apud Vergilium intellegi posse. Tumidum est: o)/reos o)/ros a)pospa=tai. Vergilius quid ait? rapit haud partem exiguam montis. Ita a magnitudine discedit, ut non inprudenter discedat a fide. Est inflatum: kai\ kai/ria ba/lletai nh=ssos.
passages.english: The most corrupt thing of all that has ever been said, since eloquent men began to go mad, they used to think was the line of Dorion in his paraphrase of Homer, when the blinded Cyclops hurled the rock back into the sea. How such things may pass from corrupt expressions to a point where they are both grand and yet sound, Maecenas used to say, can be understood from Vergil. It is bombastic [to say]: "a mountain is torn from a mountain." What does Vergil say? "He snatches no small part of a mountain." So he departs from grandeur in such a way that he does not unwisely depart from credibility. It is inflated [to say]: "and an island is hurled with deadly aim."
passages.notes: The Greek quotations are transliterated in the edition (Beta Code). The second, kai\ kai/ria ba/lletai nh=ssos, appears corrupt; the translation takes kai/ria as "with deadly aim", but the sense is uncertain. The passage seems to lack a quotation of Dorion's line after "into the sea".

passages.original: Haec sunt, inquit, quae uos confundunt: hostes, sociorum fuga, paucitas. Non quidem in hac suasoria sed in hac materia disertissima illa fertur sententia DORIONIS , cum posuisset hoc dixisse trecentis Leonidam quod puto etiam apud Herodotum esse a)ristopoiei=sqai w(s e)n a(/|dou deipnhsome/nous.
passages.english: "These are the things," he said, "that dismay you: the enemy, the flight of the allies, our small numbers." Not indeed in this suasoria, but on this theme, that most eloquent sententia of Dorion is reported, when he had represented Leonidas as having said to the three hundred (which I think is also in Herodotus): "Eat your breakfast as men who will dine in Hades."
passages.notes: The Greek is given in Beta Code transliteration.

passages.original: at nunc cuilibet orationes in Verrem tuto dicere licet pro suo. Sed ut sciatis sensum bene dictum dici tamen posse melius, notate prae ceteris quanto decentius Vergilius dixerit hoc quod ualde erat celebre “belli mora concidit Hector:” Quidquid ad aduersae cessatum est moenia Troiae Hectoris Aeneaeque manu uictoria Graium Haesit. MESSALA aiebat hic Vergilium debuisse desinere: quod sequitur Et in decimum uestigia rettulit annum, explementum esse, Maecenas hoc etiam priori conparabat.
passages.english: But now anyone may safely deliver the speeches against Verres as his own. But so that you may know that a thought well expressed can nevertheless be expressed better, note above all how much more becomingly Vergil said what was very famous, "in Hector the delay of the war fell": "Whatever delay there was at the walls of hostile Troy, by the hand of Hector and Aeneas the victory of the Greeks was held back." Messala used to say that Vergil ought to have stopped here; that what follows, "and turned its steps back into the tenth year," is padding. Maecenas compared this too with the earlier [version].
passages.notes: The opening sentence lacks its preceding context.

passages.original: Apud Caesarem cum mentio esset de ingenio Hateri consuetudine prolapsus dixit: “et ille erat plena deo.” quaerenti deinde quid hoc esse uellet uersum Vergilii retulit et quomodo hoc semel sibi apud Messalam excidisset et nunquam non postea potuisset excidere. Tiberius ipse Theodoreus offendebatur Nicetis ingenio, itaque delectatus est fabula Gallionis: hoc autem dicebat Gallio Nasoni suo ualde placuisse; itaque fecisse illum quod in multis aliis uersibus Vergilii fecerat, non subripiendi causa, sed palam mutuandi, hoc animo ut uellet agnosci; esse autem in tragoedia eius: feror huc illuc, ut plena deo.
passages.english: At Caesar's court, when mention was made of the talent of Haterius, [someone], slipping from habit, said: "and he was full of the god." Then, when [Caesar] asked what he meant by this, he cited the line of Vergil, and how this had once escaped him at Messala's house and afterwards had never failed to escape him. Tiberius himself, a Theodorean, was offended by the style of Nicetes, and so was delighted by Gallio's story. Gallio used to say that this [phrase] had greatly pleased his friend Naso; and that therefore he had done what he had done with many other lines of Vergil, not for the sake of stealing, but of borrowing openly, with the intention that it should be recognised; and that in his tragedy there is: "I am borne here and there, like one full of the god."
passages.notes: The text seems disordered or lacunose: the speaker who 'slipped' is unnamed (probably Gallio), and the sentence about Tiberius and Nicetes may be misplaced.

passages.original: Valde in uos contumeliosus fuero, si totam controuersiam quam ego intellego me dicere cum FVSCVS declamaret et a parte aui non agnoscentis puerum tractaret locum contra somnia et deorum prouidentiam, et male de magnitudine eorum dixisset mereri eum qui illos circa puerperas mitteret, summis clamoribus illum dixit Vergili uersum:
passages.english: I shall be very insulting to you if [I recount] the whole controversia, which I understand I am speaking of. When Fuscus was declaiming it and, on the side of the grandfather who did not acknowledge the boy, was handling the commonplace against dreams and the providence of the gods, and had said that he who sent them to attend women in childbirth was doing ill service to their majesty, he spoke, amid the loudest applause, that line of Vergil:
passages.notes: The first sentence is syntactically incomplete and probably corrupt; a verb (e.g. 'repeat') seems to be missing.

passages.original: Scilicet is superis labor est, ea cura quietos Sollicitat. Auditor FVSCI quidam cuius pudori parco, cum hanc suasoriam de Alexandro ante Fuscum diceret, putabat aeque belle poni eundem uersum et dixit: Scilicet is superis labor est, ea cura quietos Sollicitat. FVSCVS illi ait: si hoc dixisses audiente Alexandro, scisses apud Vergilium et illum uersum esse: capulo tenus abdidit ensem. Et quia soletis mihi molesti esse de FVSCO, quid fuerit, quare nemo uideretur dixisse cultius, ingeram uobis Fuscinas explicationes. Dicebat autem suasorias libentissime et frequentius Graecas quam Latinas.
passages.english: "Surely this is a labour for the gods above, this care troubles their calm." A certain pupil of Fuscus, whose shame I spare, when he was delivering this suasoria about Alexander before Fuscus, thought the same line could be used just as nicely, and said: "Surely this is a labour for the gods above, this care troubles their calm." Fuscus said to him: "If you had said this in Alexander's hearing, you would have learned that there is also this line in Vergil: 'he buried his sword up to the hilt.'" And since you are always pestering me about Fuscus, about what it was that made no one seem to speak more elegantly, I shall heap Fuscus' descriptive passages upon you. He used to deliver suasoriae most willingly, and more often Greek ones than Latin.

passages.original: Sciant posteri potuisse Antonio seruire rempublicam, non potuisse Ciceronem. Laudandus erit tibi Antonius: in hac causa etiam Ciceronem uerba deficient. Crede mihi, quam diligenter te custodieris faciet tamen Antonius quod Cicero tacere non possit. Si intellegis, Cicero, non dicit “roga ut uiuas,” sed “roga ut seruias.” Quemadmodum autem hunc senatum intrare poteris, exhaustum crudeliter, repletum turpiter? intrare autem tu senatum uoles in quo non Cn. Pompeium uisurus es, non M.
passages.english: Let posterity know that the republic could be a slave to Antony, but Cicero could not. You will have to praise Antony: in this cause even Cicero will lack words. Believe me, however carefully you guard yourself, Antony will still do something about which Cicero cannot keep silent. If you understand, Cicero, he is not saying "beg to live," but "beg to be a slave." And how will you be able to enter this senate, cruelly drained, shamefully refilled? And will you want to enter a senate in which you will not see Gnaeus Pompey, nor Marcus
passages.notes: The final sentence continues into the following context ("Cato...").

passages.original: Ergo loquitur umquam Cicero ut non timeat Antonius, loquitur umquam Antonius ut Cicero timeat? Ciuilis sanguinis Syllana sitis in ciuitatem redit, et ad triumuiralem hastam pro uectigalibus ciuium manorum mortes locantur;
passages.english: So does Cicero ever speak without Antony being afraid, and does Antony ever speak so that Cicero is afraid? The Sullan thirst for citizen blood returns to the state, and at the triumviral spear, in place of the revenues, the deaths of Roman citizens are put out to contract;
passages.notes: 'manorum' is read as 'Romanorum'. The 'spear' is the sign of a public auction.

passages.original: uix medius fidius Oceanus tot res tamque diuersas uno tempore absorbere potuisset.” Huic tu saeuienti putas Ciceronem posse subduci? ARELLI FVSCI patris. Ab armis ad arma discurritur: foris uictores domi trucidamur, domi in sanguine intestinus hostis incubat: quis non hoc populi Romani statu Ciceronem ut uiuat cogi putat? Rogabis, Cicero, turpiter Antonium, et frustra. Non te ignobilis tumulus abscondet; idem uirtutis tuae qui finis est mortalium. humanorum operum custos memoria, quae magnis uiris uitam perpetuat, in omnia te saecula sacratum dabit:
passages.english: by heaven, Ocean itself could scarcely have swallowed so many and such different things at one time." Do you think Cicero can be removed from the reach of this raging man? [From] Arellius Fuscus the father: There is running from arms to arms: victors abroad, we are slaughtered at home; at home an enemy within broods in blood. Who, in this state of the Roman people, thinks Cicero is to be compelled to live? You will beg Antony, Cicero, shamefully, and in vain. No obscure tomb will hide you; the end of your virtue is not the same as that of mortals. Memory, the guardian of human works, which perpetuates the life of great men, will hand you down hallowed to all ages:
passages.notes: 'idem uirtutis tuae qui finis est mortalium' seems corrupt; a negative is probably lost ('non idem'), and it is translated so.

passages.original: Proscriptus est ille qui tuam sententiam secutus est: tota tabula tuae morti proluditur; alter fratrem proscribi, alter auunculum patitur: quid habes spei? ut Cicero periret tot parricidia facta sunt. Repetas tecum tot patrocinia, tot clientelas et maximum beneficiorum tuorum, rempublicam ipsam: iam intelleges Ciceronem in mortem cogi posse, in preces non posse.
passages.english: The man who followed your proposal has been proscribed; the whole list is a prelude to your death; one allows his brother to be proscribed, the other his uncle: what hope do you have? So that Cicero might perish, so many parricides have been committed. Go over in your mind so many defences, so many clienteles, and the greatest of your benefactions, the republic itself: you will then understand that Cicero can be forced to death, but not to entreaties.

passages.original: etiamsi impetrare uitam ab Antonio potes, non est tanti rogare; deinde: impetrare non potes. In priore illa parte posuit turpe esse cuilibet Romano, nedum Ciceroni, uitam rogare: hoc loco omnium qui ultro mortem adprehendissent exempla posuit. deinde: inutilis uita futura et morte grauior detracta libertate. hic omnem acerbitatem seruitutis futurae descripsit.
passages.english: even if you can obtain your life from Antony, it is not worth the asking; next: you cannot obtain it. In that first part he argued that it was shameful for any Roman, let alone Cicero, to beg for his life; at this point he set out the examples of all those who had embraced death of their own accord. Next: life would be useless, and heavier than death, once liberty had been taken away. Here he described all the bitterness of the slavery to come.

passages.original: Sed ad diuisionem CESTI reuertamur. Dixit utile esse, ne etiam cruciatus corporis pateretur: non simplici illum modo periturum, si in Antonii manibus incidisset. in hac parte cum descripsisset contumelias insultantium Ciceroni et uerbera et tormenta, dixit illam multum laudatam sententiam: tum mehercules, Cicero, cum ueneris ad Antonium, mortem rogabis.
passages.english: But let us return to the division of Cestius. He said it was expedient [to die], so that he should not also suffer torture of the body: he would not perish in a simple manner if he fell into Antony's hands. In this part, after describing the insults of those mocking Cicero, and the beatings and tortures, he spoke that much-praised epigram: "Then, by Hercules, Cicero, when you come to Antony, you will beg for death."

passages.original: Alteram partem pauci declamauerunt. nemo ausus est Ciceronem ad deprecandum Antonium hortari, bene de Ciceronis animo iudicauerunt. GEMINVS VARIVS declamauit alteram quoque partem et ait: spero me Ciceroni meo persuasurum ut uelit uiuere. quod grandia loquitur et dicit: “mors nec immatura consulari nec misera sapienti,” non mouet me: ideo tamen non peribit; ego belle mores hominis noui: faciet, rogabit. nam quod ad seruitutem pertinet, non recusabit; iam collum tritum habet; et Pompeius illum et Caesar subiecerunt: ueteranum mancipium uidetis.
passages.english: Few declaimed the other side. No one dared to urge Cicero to plead with Antony; they judged rightly of Cicero's spirit. Geminus Varius declaimed the other side as well, and said: "I hope I shall persuade my Cicero to be willing to live. That he talks grandly and says, 'Death is neither untimely for an ex-consul nor wretched for a wise man,' does not move me: he will not perish for all that; I know the man's character nicely: he will do it, he will beg. For as regards slavery, he will not refuse it; his neck is already worn by the yoke; both Pompey and Caesar have subdued him: you see a veteran slave."

passages.original: satisfaciam uobis et fortasse efficiam, ut his sententiis lectis solidis et uerum habentibus a scolasticis recedatis: sed quia, hoc si iam recta uia consequi non potero, decipere uos cogar, uelut salutarem daturus pueris potionem absinthiati poculi, LIVIVS adeo retractationis consilium habuisse Ciceronem non dicit, ut neget tempus habuisse; ita enim ait:
passages.english: I will satisfy you, and perhaps bring it about that, once you have read these solid and truthful sayings, you will withdraw from the schoolmen; but because, if I cannot achieve this by the straight road, I shall be forced to trick you, like someone about to give children a healthful drink in a cup of wormwood: Livy is so far from saying that Cicero had any thought of recantation that he denies he had the time; for he speaks thus:
passages.notes: The construction of the sentence is loose and the text possibly disturbed; the 'cup of wormwood' image (giving medicine disguised) is rendered literally.

passages.original: CREMVTIVS CORDVS et ipse ait Ciceronem secum cogitasse, utrumne Brutum, an Cassium, an Sex. Pompeium peteret, set omnia illi displicuisse praeter mortem. CREMVTI CORDI. Quibus uisis laetus Antonius, cum peractam proscriptionem suam dixisset esse, quippe non satiatus modo caedendis ciuibus, sed differtus quoque, super rostra exponit.
passages.english: Cremutius Cordus too says that Cicero considered with himself whether he should make for Brutus, or Cassius, or Sextus Pompeius, but that everything displeased him except death. [From] Cremutius Cordus: "Antony, delighted at the sight of these, having declared that his proscription was complete, since he was not merely sated with the slaughter of citizens but even stuffed full, displays them above the Rostra."
passages.notes: 'these' refers to Cicero's severed head and hands, mentioned before the excerpt begins.

passages.original: POLLIO quoque ASINIVS , qui Verrem Ciceronis reum fortissime morientem tradidit, Ciceronis mortem solus ex omnibus maligne narrat; testimonium tamen quamuis inuitus plenum ei reddidit. Asini Pollionis. “Huius ergo uiri tot tantisque operibus mansuris in omne aeuum praedicare de ingenio atque industria superuacuum est.
passages.english: Asinius Pollio also, who recorded that Verres, Cicero's defendant, died most bravely, alone of all narrates Cicero's death spitefully; yet even against his will he rendered him full testimony. [From] Asinius Pollio: "Of this man, then, whose works are so many and so great and will endure for all time, it is superfluous to proclaim his genius and industry.

passages.original: Non fraudabo municipem nostrum bono uersu, ex quo hic multo melior SEVERI CORNELII processit: Conticuit Latiae tristis facundia linguae. SEXTILIVS ENA fuit homo ingeniosus magis quam eruditus, inaequalis poeta et plane quibusdam locis talis, quales esse Cicero Cordubenses poetas ait, pingue quiddam sonantis atque peregrinum. is hanc ipsam proscriptionem recitaturus in domo Messalae Coruini Pollionem Asinium aduocauerat, et in principio hunc uersum non sine assensu recitauit: Deflendus Cicero est Latiaeque silentia linguae.
passages.english: I will not cheat our fellow townsman of a good line, from which this much better one of Cornelius Severus derived: "Silent, in sorrow, fell the eloquence of the Latin tongue." Sextilius Ena was a man more gifted than learned, an uneven poet, and in certain passages plainly of the kind Cicero says the poets of Corduba are, sounding something thick and foreign. When about to recite on this very proscription in the house of Messalla Corvinus, he had invited Asinius Pollio, and at the beginning he recited this line, not without applause: "Cicero must be wept for, and the silence of the Latin tongue."

passages.original: nunc ut scias nihil esse melius quam mori, uitam tibi Antonius promittit. Pendet nefariae proscriptionis tabula: tot praetorii, tot consulares, tot equestris ordinis uiri periere; nemo relinquitur nisi qui seruire possit. nescio an hoc tempore uiuere uelis, Cicero: nemo est cum quo uelis. Merito, hercules, illo tempore uixisti quo Caesar ultro te rogauit ut uiueres sine ulla pactione, quo tempore non quidem stabat respublica, sed in boni principis sinum ceciderat.
passages.english: Now, so that you may know that nothing is better than to die, Antony promises you life. The tablet of the wicked proscription hangs up: so many ex-praetors, so many ex-consuls, so many men of the equestrian order have perished; no one is left except those who can be slaves. I doubt whether you would want to live at this time, Cicero: there is no one with whom you would want to. Rightly, by Hercules, you lived in that time when Caesar of his own accord asked you to live, without any bargain, a time when the republic did not indeed stand, but had fallen into the lap of a good leader.

passages.original: P. ASPRENATIS. Vt Antonius Ciceroni parcat, Cicero in eloquentiam suam ipse animaduertet? quid autem tibi sub ista pactione promittitur? ut Cn. Pompeius et M. Cato et ille antiquos restituatur reipublicae senatus, dignissimus apud quem Cicero loqueretur?
passages.english: [From] Publius Asprenas: So that Antony may spare Cicero, will Cicero himself punish his own eloquence? And what is promised you under that bargain? That Gnaeus Pompey and Marcus Cato and that senate of old, most worthy to have Cicero speak before it, will be restored to the republic?

passages.original: Mortem tibi remittit, ut id pereat quod in te solum inmortale est. qualis est pactio ? aufertur Ciceroni ingenium sine uita; promittuntur pro obliuione nominis tui pauci seruitutis anni. Non ille te uiuere uult, sed tacere ingenii tui superstitem. Viue, ut Cicero audiat Lepidum, Cicero audiat Antonium, nemo Ciceronem. Poteris perferre, ut quod Cicero optimum habet ante se efferat? sine durare post te ingenium tuum, perpetuam Antonii proscriptionem. ARELLI FVSCI patris.
passages.english: He remits death for you, so that what alone in you is immortal may perish. What sort of bargain is this? Cicero is robbed of his genius without [losing] his life; in exchange for the oblivion of your name a few years of slavery are promised. He does not want you to live, but to be silent, outliving your genius. Live, so that Cicero may listen to Lepidus, Cicero may listen to Antony, and no one to Cicero. Will you be able to endure carrying out to burial before you the best thing Cicero has? Let your genius endure after you, a perpetual proscription of Antony. [From] Arellius Fuscus the father.
passages.notes: 'efferat' is the technical term for carrying out a corpse for burial.

passages.original: Huius suasoriae alteram partem neminem scio declamasse; omnes pro libris Ciceronis solliciti fuerunt, nemo pro ipso, cum adeo illa pars non sit mala, ut Cicero, si haec condicio lata ei fuisset, deliberaturus non fuerit. Itaque hanc suasoriam nemo declamauit efficacius quam Silo Pompeius: non enim ad illa speciosa se contulit ad quae CESTIVS qui dixit, hoc grauius esse supplicium quam mortem, et ideo hoc Antonium eligere;
passages.english: I know of no one who declaimed the other side of this suasoria; all were anxious for Cicero's books, none for the man himself, although that side is not so bad that Cicero, had this condition been put to him, would not have deliberated over it. And so no one declaimed this suasoria more effectively than Pompeius Silo: for he did not betake himself to those showy arguments to which Cestius [resorted], who said that this was a heavier punishment than death, and that for this reason Antony chose it;
passages.notes: The sentence is incomplete in the text and continues beyond the passage. 'ad quae CESTIVS qui dixit' is awkward; the text may be corrupt or have lost a word (e.g. a verb such as 'se contulit'). I have rendered the sense.

passages.original: non esse tam stultum Antonium, ut putaret ad rem pertinere libros a Cicerone conburi, cuius scripta per totum orbem terrarum celebrarentur, nec hoc petere eum quod posset ipse facere: nisi forte non esset in scripta Ciceronis ei ius cui esset in Ciceronem; quaeri nihil aliud quam ut ille Cicero multa fortiter de mortis contemptu locutus ad turpes condiciones perductus occideretur. Antonium illi non uitam cum condicione promittere, sed mortem sub infamia quaerere. Itaque quod turpiter postea passurus esset nunc illum debere fortiter pati.
passages.english: [he said] that Antony was not so foolish as to think it mattered that the books be burned by Cicero, whose writings were celebrated throughout the whole world, nor was he asking for what he could do himself, unless perhaps he did not have the same power over Cicero's writings that he had over Cicero; what was sought was nothing other than that the great Cicero, who had spoken boldly and at length about despising death, should be brought to shameful terms and then killed. Antony was not promising him life on a condition, but seeking his death under disgrace. And so what he would later suffer shamefully he ought now to suffer bravely.
passages.notes: The passage continues Silo's argument in indirect speech, so the subject of the infinitives is Silo's speech ('he said').
